The result was a console that combines radical innovation with cost-effectiveness. In there, users found imaginative interaction methods while developers had to deal with the legacy technology underneath them.</p><p>The new issue of the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/">Architecture of consoles</a> has arrived. This time, we take a look at what would be Nintendo’s <em>last</em> joint project with IBM and AMD.</p><h3 id="references-to-its-predecessor-and-competitor">References to its predecessor and competitor</h3><p>You’d be surprised that the Wii U shares its DNA with two somewhat distinct consoles: The <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/wii/">Wii</a> and the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/xbox-360/">Xbox 360</a> (which, in turn, inherit technology from the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/gamecube/">GameCube</a> and the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation-3/">PlayStation 3</a>!). For that reason, I strongly recommend you read those write-ups first, as many of the technologies introduced here are related to their predecessors.</p><p>Furthermore, Wii backwards compatibility is a recurrent topic of this article. In contrast with the software emulation on the Xbox 360 and the provisional PS2 hardware on the PlayStation 3, the Wii U takes it to an obsessive level. It does come at a cost, though, which you’ll eventually see as well. In any case, the main goal of this article is to analyse the Wii U. So, Wii-related capabilities will be discussed separately from the main functions.</p><hr><h2 id="next-gen-controller">Next-gen controller</h2><p>When it comes to Nintendo, the controller tends to be an engaging topic of discussion. Here is no exception, so I found it more captivating to start the analysis with this component before we dive into the main box.</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/gamepad.20bb73ea5e39a872fbaaf3b9cfbffd5a57c88c61897abe07d4173d9e2f53fe5b.jpg"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/gamepad.20bb73ea5e39a872fbaaf3b9cfbffd5a57c88c61897abe07d4173d9e2f53fe5b_hu_1fc43a25e0908657.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/gamepad.20bb73ea5e39a872fbaaf3b9cfbffd5a57c88c61897abe07d4173d9e2f53fe5b_hu_463388bc0457570d.webp 800w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/gamepad.20bb73ea5e39a872fbaaf3b9cfbffd5a57c88c61897abe07d4173d9e2f53fe5b_hu_ec5575f97fd826c3.webp 1000w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="1000" height="579" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/gamepad.20bb73ea5e39a872fbaaf3b9cfbffd5a57c88c61897abe07d4173d9e2f53fe5b.jpg" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">The GamePad (black edition).</figcaption></figure><p>The Wii U comes with a single wireless ‘controller’ (albeit nothing like seen before). It’s twice the size of a traditional controller but bundles twice the functionality. Its technical name is <strong>Display Remote Controller</strong> (DRC) but users better know it as <strong>GamePad</strong>. In there, we find a touchscreen, a set of buttons, a hidden stylus and many, many sensors. All in all, it’s one interesting <em>brick</em>.</p><p>Due to its abundance of hardware, you could consider it an independent computer by itself. However, due to its software, the GamePad ultimately behaves as a <strong>terminal linked to the console</strong>, with duties including:</p><ul><li><strong>Input device</strong> by forwarding sensor data and button presses to the console.</li><li><strong>Output device</strong> by receiving audio and video streams from the console and reproducing them on the internal display and speakers.</li><li><strong>Signal processing</strong> by seamlessly encoding and decoding data streams travelling from or to the console.</li></ul><p>In doing so, apart from being a controller, the GamePad was marketed with two functionalities in mind: A ‘second screen’ and a ‘mirror screen’. In the first case, the console may display exclusive information on the GamePad without consuming TV space. In the other, the user may use the console without requiring a TV anymore.</p><div class="side-by-side"><figure class="toleft"><a class="toleft" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/zelda_extended.df7a8a0b72c77d8f35b5deea821bbf1b3411953ccea56468c6da915005c1c9d4.jpg"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/zelda_extended.df7a8a0b72c77d8f35b5deea821bbf1b3411953ccea56468c6da915005c1c9d4_hu_4c4c7f242207bb0a.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/zelda_extended.df7a8a0b72c77d8f35b5deea821bbf1b3411953ccea56468c6da915005c1c9d4_hu_491e77b52495367c.webp 800w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/zelda_extended.df7a8a0b72c77d8f35b5deea821bbf1b3411953ccea56468c6da915005c1c9d4_hu_2078361c7eb006b6.webp 1200w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="1200" height="685" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/zelda_extended.df7a8a0b72c77d8f35b5deea821bbf1b3411953ccea56468c6da915005c1c9d4.jpg" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">The Legend of Zelda: Twilight Princess HD (2016).<br>The GamePad’s display acts as a handy secondary screen to show the map and inventory.</figcaption></figure><figure class="toright"><a class="toright" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/mario_mirrored.15d3e146de0b09d0bb3cb7c7f15bf2a17517e4f4934e023d34c9cf12cc6937a2.jpg"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/mario_mirrored.15d3e146de0b09d0bb3cb7c7f15bf2a17517e4f4934e023d34c9cf12cc6937a2_hu_815f12f04cd294c8.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/mario_mirrored.15d3e146de0b09d0bb3cb7c7f15bf2a17517e4f4934e023d34c9cf12cc6937a2_hu_f9de1bdb80676ebd.webp 800w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/mario_mirrored.15d3e146de0b09d0bb3cb7c7f15bf2a17517e4f4934e023d34c9cf12cc6937a2_hu_107c16d5c0bdd715.webp 1200w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="1200" height="685" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/mario_mirrored.15d3e146de0b09d0bb3cb7c7f15bf2a17517e4f4934e023d34c9cf12cc6937a2.jpg" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Super Mario Maker (2015).<br>Main gameplay happens on the GamePad, the TV just acts as a ‘projector’.</figcaption></figure></div><p>In practice, however, there wasn’t any standardisation in place. So, the adoption of either style completely depended on how the game was programmed.</p><h3 id="architecture">Architecture</h3><p>Let’s now see what the GamePad is made of, a tricky task by itself since the internals of the GamePad aren’t documented whatsoever. Luckily, a hacking group called ‘Memahaxx’ took matters into their own hands and completely reversed-engineered the device. If that wasn’t enough, they also took the time to share their discoveries with the public.</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/gamepad/overview.cfdbd79aa2b87ab955185339e91c3a88fc4aca03ec1f71eaf3bd3e79907a4ce5.png"><picture><img class="title-image no-borders" alt="Image" width="1188" height="804" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/gamepad/overview.cfdbd79aa2b87ab955185339e91c3a88fc4aca03ec1f71eaf3bd3e79907a4ce5.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">The internal architecture of the GamePad.</figcaption></figure><p>The device bundles three main chips <sup id="bibref:1"><a href="#bib:io-controller_overview" role="doc-biblioref">[1]</a></sup> or, better yet, three independent computers:</p><p>Firstly, we’ve got <strong>DRC-WUP</strong> which is a System-on-Chip (SoC) hiding yet-another <strong>ARM926EJ-S</strong> (the same one from the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/wii/#the-hidden-co-processor">Wii</a>, <em>how many of these do they have in stock?</em>) along with <strong>4 MB of RAM</strong> and a special <strong>H.264 accelerator</strong> for encoding and decoding H.264 streams. This is the main chip that controls the peripheral. It has access to the screen, audio and NFC functionality.</p><p>Next to the SoC, you’ll find the <strong>Broadcom BCM4319</strong>, another tiny computer that houses an <strong>ARM Cortex-M3</strong> and the radio-frequency infrastructure that provides <strong>802.11 a/b/g/n</strong> connectivity <sup id="bibref:2"><a href="#bib:io-controller_bc" role="doc-biblioref">[2]</a></sup>. It’s worth emphasising that Broadcom’s choice of CPU is a bit more ‘contemporary’ than Nintendo’s, considering that the Cortex-M3 (with its second version of <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/game-boy-advance/#tab-2-3-squeezing-performance">Thumb</a>) was designed for embedded systems of the 2010s decade. To be fair, it’s known that Nintendo’s choices are not always based on ‘cutting-edginess’ but on cost and supply. In any case, the BCM4319 will be providing Wi-Fi connectivity using the 5 GHz band.</p><p>Finally, <strong>UIC-WUP</strong> is another Nintendo-branded component where we can find an <strong>STMicroelectronics STM8</strong>, <strong>2 KB and 28 KB of EEPROM</strong>. The STM8 is one of those modern 8-bit microcontrollers used for small but repetitive tasks. That said, UIC-WUP is delegated with handling the remaining I/O.</p><p>The GamePad’s firmware (or firmwares) are stored in a separate Flash chip. This provides <strong>32 MB</strong> worth of space accessed through an SPI bus. Curiously enough, the firmware code <strong>is not encrypted</strong> (facilitating the work of Memahaxx).</p><p>The rest of the GamePad’s motherboard is filled with I/O endpoints and unusual sensors. So, I will go over them in the ‘I/O’ part of this article.</p><h4 id="talking-to-the-mothership">Talking to the mothership</h4><p>The Wii U’s motherboard includes a tiny chip called <strong>DRH</strong> which relies on the Wi-Fi protocol to communicate with the GamePad and the USB protocol to communicate with the rest of the motherboard. This includes the GPU, which streams frame-buffers directly to the DRH so they get displayed on the GamePad.</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/gamepad/connections.ae9e8e202a676efb7f8eec06fa72cf6172988315babeb545a44a423d488afb74.png"><picture><img class="title-image no-borders" alt="Image" width="1289" height="408" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/gamepad/connections.ae9e8e202a676efb7f8eec06fa72cf6172988315babeb545a44a423d488afb74.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Overview of the GamePad-Wii U connection.</figcaption></figure><p>DRH runs a Real-time Operating System (RTOS) which implements the µITRON 4.0 specification. It’s quite sophisticated, offering cooperative multitasking and inter-task communication. Finally, it’s worth noting that the Wii U-GamePad communication over Wi-Fi is not mixed with the internet capabilities of the Wii U, that’s handled by a separate chip (and antenna).</p><h3 id="background-functionality">Background functionality</h3><p>Apart from the personalised implementation of the network stack (which will be explained in a bit), the GamePad does a lot of processing behind the scenes.</p><p>Once the GamePad is up and running, the device is capable of displaying an H.264 video stream by decoding it on-the-fly. The screen resolution is <strong>854x480 pixels</strong> with a refresh rate of <strong>60 Hz</strong>, which isn’t exactly HD, but it maintains 16:9 proportionality.</p><h4 id="strange-use-of-standards">Strange use of standards</h4><p>Similarly to how the Wii Remote <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/wii/#next-gen-controllers">mangles the Bluetooth protocol</a> to avoid third-party usage, the GamePad breaks two Wi-Fi standards, namely WPS and WPA2-PSK, so they only work with the Wii U <sup id="bibref:3"><a href="#bib:io-controller_wifi" role="doc-biblioref">[3]</a></sup>.</p><p>In summary, the Wii U and the GamePad communicate with each other using <strong>802.11n in the 5 GHz band</strong>. The console acts as an access point (AP) and the GamePad acts as its single client. Be as it may, Memahaxx also reported that the console’s operating system implemented the possibility of using two GamePads at once, albeit left unused.</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/setup.c083e0e65d990f3debb8855c468cfd5d28356494e007e5205ce86ea2a83c1481.jpg"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/setup.c083e0e65d990f3debb8855c468cfd5d28356494e007e5205ce86ea2a83c1481_hu_3014fea467a19ae0.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/setup.c083e0e65d990f3debb8855c468cfd5d28356494e007e5205ce86ea2a83c1481_hu_b249a6ebdf01af09.webp 800w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/setup.c083e0e65d990f3debb8855c468cfd5d28356494e007e5205ce86ea2a83c1481_hu_1b0e8d7026b1b6bf.webp 1200w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="1200" height="693" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/setup.c083e0e65d990f3debb8855c468cfd5d28356494e007e5205ce86ea2a83c1481.jpg" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">The process of pairing a GamePad with the Wii U involves the user entering a password made of Poker card symbols.</figcaption></figure><p>To establish a communication channel for the first time, both devices must be ‘paired’ first (in the same way a Windows laptop pairs with the Wi-Fi router by selecting the network name and supplying a password). This is done using the <strong>Wi-Fi Protected Setup</strong> (WPS) protocol, however, it’s not as easy as pressing the <code>SYNC</code> button and waiting until both devices pair. The process also involves the user selecting specific poker symbols shown on the GamePad as instructed on the TV (rendered by the console). Behind the scenes, the user is inputting part of the password, the GamePad then adds a hardcoded <code>5678</code> at the end of the password and sends it to the console. If the process has finished successfully, the GamePad receives the console’s SSID, BSSID and PSK values so it can automatically connect from now on.</p><p>From there on, subsequent connections rely on the <strong>WPA2-PSK</strong> protocol and both devices transfer their information using TCP/IP packets.</p><p>As a curious fact, the GamePad takes advantage of <strong>timestamps</strong> to keep Audio and Video streams synchronised. Timestamps are an attribute found on ‘Beacon Frames’, broadcast by access points for many reasons, one of which is to synchronise the internal clocks of in-range devices.</p><hr><h2 id="cpu">CPU</h2><p>I hope you’ve got some time left as we still have to check out the internals of the Wii U, starting with the <em>central</em> chip.</p><h3 id="origins-and-hypotheses">Origins and hypotheses</h3><p>Since the Wii U was announced (then known as <strong>Project Cafe</strong>), there’s been significant speculation about what would the new CPU be made of. At some point, journalists speculated that Nintendo would embrace a modern version of IBM’s <strong>POWER</strong> line <sup id="bibref:4"><a href="#bib:cpu-early_cpu" role="doc-biblioref">[4]</a></sup>. I guess audiences were expecting a ground-breaking CPU as Cell and Xenon proved six years before. Moreover, with the decline of PowerPC (most apparently with Apple switching to <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/xbox/#p6-and-the-end-of-pentium-numbers">Intel Core</a> in 2006), the idea that any new CPU from IBM would come as a derivative of POWER wasn’t too far-fetched.</p><p>Well, there is one fault with the previous logic, which is that <strong>Nintendo doesn’t favour emerging technology</strong>. Their formula focuses instead on grabbing existing technology and finding innovative and clever uses. This is not necessarily a bad characteristic, as Nintendo engineers have been very clever in showing state-of-the-art applications with technology deemed ‘outdated’. Take a look at the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/game-boy/#cpu">Z80-hybrid</a> of a Game Boy, or the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/nintendo-ds/#tab-1-2-arm946e-s">under-clocked ARM9</a> on the Nintendo DS, or even the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/wii/#cpu">partially-updated</a> GameCube called ‘Wii’. If there’s something common among all of these, is that all have broken sales records. Now, will the Wii U be part of that club? You’ll be the judge of that.</p><h3 id="the-8th-generation-architecture">The 8th-generation architecture</h3><p>In the past generation, Sony and Microsoft made strong bets (some riskier than others) on contemporary technologies at a reduced cost. With the Wii U, Nintendo looked at a slightly different direction, focusing on low-cost, low-power consumption and backwards compatibility <sup id="bibref:5"><a href="#bib:games-devsecrets" role="doc-biblioref">[5]</a></sup>. The latter will have a strong impact on the final design of this console. Consequently, the new CPU doesn’t deliver any radical component and instead tries to catch up with the latest advancements in the industry (multi-core processing, GHz speeds, etc).</p><p>That being said, Nintendo partnered with IBM to deliver their new CPU. The result was <strong>Espresso</strong> and runs at <strong>1.24 GHz</strong> <sup id="bibref:6"><a href="#bib:cpu-fail0verflow" role="doc-biblioref">[6]</a></sup>.</p><p>Now, let’s bring Espresso forward:</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/espresso/espresso.add469b7e627cb2a1aa292b687af9d3e5eacdf5f194fd6e0ad034aee2cfdfec7.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="764" height="450" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/espresso/espresso.add469b7e627cb2a1aa292b687af9d3e5eacdf5f194fd6e0ad034aee2cfdfec7.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Overview of Espresso.</figcaption></figure><p>… and as with any other article in this series, I’ll explain how it works.</p><h4 id="familiar-faces">Familiar faces</h4><p>Before we start the real analysis, let me go back to the previous diagram. As you’ve seen there, Espresso is a symmetric multi-core system, just like <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/xbox-360/#cpu">Xenon</a>. But that’s not all, as each of Espresso’s cores appears to be a <strong>replica of IBM’s <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/wii/#cpu">Broadway</a></strong>, the exact same core used with the Wii (which in turn, is a tweaked version of <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/gamecube/#cpu">Gekko</a>, found in the GameCube).</p><h3 id="study-of-espresso">Study of Espresso</h3><p>We’ll now take a look at how Espresso is constructed. As I’ve already explained how <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/wii/#cpu">Broadway</a> and <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/gamecube/#cpu">Gekko</a> work, I’ll focus on the novelties of Espresso, namely its multi-core layout, cache system and memory.</p><p>At this point, it’s fair to say that neither Nintendo nor IBM have publicly documented the inner workings of Espresso (unlike Xenon and Cell from which many IBM engineers published papers on IBM’s now-defunct developerWorks portal). I guess that neither planned to commercialise Espresso outside the Wii U. As a consequence, this section has been possible due to the countless hours spent by hacking groups like fail0verflow (a.k.a Team Twiizers) which not only managed to reverse-engineer this system, but also take the time to publish documentation about it (don’t forget to look at the cited documents if you enjoy the topic). For this study, I’ve combined third-party research with public information from IBM (related to Broadway) and Freescale, and the result is what you see below.</p><div class="tabs"><ul class="tab-links"><li id="tab-1-1-multi-coring-broadway-link" class="active"><a href="#tab-1-1-multi-coring-broadway">‘Multi-coring’ Broadway</a></li><li id="tab-1-2-a-recallable-bus-link"><a href="#tab-1-2-a-recallable-bus">A recallable bus</a></li><li id="tab-1-3-more-cache-link"><a href="#tab-1-3-more-cache">More cache</a></li><li id="tab-1-4-room-for-improvement-link"><a href="#tab-1-4-room-for-improvement">Room for improvement</a></li></ul><div class="tab-content"><div class="tab active body-side" id="tab-1-1-multi-coring-broadway"><h4 id="tab-1-1-multi-coring-broadway" class="tab-title">‘Multi-coring’ Broadway</h4><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/motherboard/soc.38a8a1efada68b5df61254c204caac8a6b6705512b93c3fc7165a64a4e9f4da8.jpg"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/motherboard/soc.38a8a1efada68b5df61254c204caac8a6b6705512b93c3fc7165a64a4e9f4da8_hu_dca2e17023dfdb89.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/motherboard/soc.38a8a1efada68b5df61254c204caac8a6b6705512b93c3fc7165a64a4e9f4da8_hu_c99615761a94a3b9.webp 800w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/motherboard/soc.38a8a1efada68b5df61254c204caac8a6b6705512b93c3fc7165a64a4e9f4da8_hu_16103444ab0cc93e.webp 1000w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="1000" height="781" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/motherboard/soc.38a8a1efada68b5df61254c204caac8a6b6705512b93c3fc7165a64a4e9f4da8.jpg" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">The big SoC (housing Espresso, among others) next to four 512 MB DDR3 chips</figcaption></figure><p>Espresso bundles three CPU cores based on the <strong>PowerPC 750CXe</strong> architecture. The design of these dates all the way back to 2001, meaning that the datapath and instruction set are roughly in the same state as they were 10 years before. For comparison, the PowerPC Processing Element (the main core of Xenon and Cell) grabbed the design of the POWER4 and re-engineered it for the requirements of the respective console.</p><p>Moving on, Espresso implements a <strong>symmetric multi-core layout</strong>… but how is this possible with those old cores? Well, in a (now defunct) FAQ portal, IBM has explained that the 750 already supports a multi-processing environment <sup id="bibref:7"><a href="#bib:cpu-750faq" role="doc-biblioref">[7]</a></sup>, it just needs extra work for maintaining cache integrity (between the different L1, L2 and the TLB). However, doing this through software cancels out the advantages of having a multi-processor design, so the idea was never taken forward… That is, until Nintendo reached IBM again.</p><p>In the end, IBM grabbed three Broadway CPUs, stepped up the clock to 1.24 GHz and wrapped them with extra L2 cache and the necessary circuitry to arbitrate bus contention and cache coherency (so it doesn’t have to be done with software). That’s Espresso.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev pre">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-1-2-a-recallable-bus">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-1-2-a-recallable-bus"><h4 id="tab-1-2-a-recallable-bus" class="tab-title">A recallable bus</h4><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/espresso/cores.9e614f14d34c212eabf0bd440192b27bbf763f5c8f12bd908a9b3e0ce7ece80f.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="764" height="555" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/espresso/cores.9e614f14d34c212eabf0bd440192b27bbf763f5c8f12bd908a9b3e0ce7ece80f.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Layout of the internal cores of Espresso</figcaption></figure><p>The external bus that connects the CPU cores with external components has an interesting history, dating back to 1993, with the launch of the <strong>Motorola 88110</strong>. After the formation of the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/gamecube/#cpu">AIM alliance</a>, IBM and Motorola created a joint CPU based on their best inventions. IBM contributed with their POWER architecture and Motorola chipped in with the bus design of their 88110 CPU. In 1993, the PowerPC 601 was unveiled.</p><p>The PowerPC 601 featured a bus protocol called <strong>60x bus</strong>. This was quite advanced and flexible for the time, already supporting 64-bit operations, fast clock speeds, cache coherency and multiprocessor configurations (hence the fact IBM stated the 750 could work with multi-CPUs right away) <sup id="bibref:8"><a href="#bib:cpu-60x" role="doc-biblioref">[8]</a></sup>. All of this reminds me of the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/sega-saturn/#cpu">anticipation of the Hitachi SH-2</a>.</p><p>Back to the Wii U, IBM grabbed the 60x bus again to interconnect the three cores in Espresso. Additionally, they implemented a variant of the bus to connect Espresso (as a chip) with the rest of the motherboard.</p><p>If you wonder about the current adoption of the 60x bus, I’m afraid it’s been long superseded by an improved protocol called ‘MPX’ which Motorola implemented for their PowerPC 74xx line (also known as ‘G4’). The MPX bus solves deficiencies of the 60x like slow data throughputs with the use of ‘data streams’ to reduce wait states <sup id="bibref:9"><a href="#bib:cpu-mpc" role="doc-biblioref">[9]</a></sup>. IBM, on the other side, presented their ‘Elastic Interface’ bus with their PowerPC 970 line (G5) and POWER4 <sup id="bibref:10"><a href="#bib:cpu-ibm970" role="doc-biblioref">[10]</a></sup>.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-1-1-multi-coring-broadway">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-1-3-more-cache">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-1-3-more-cache"><h4 id="tab-1-3-more-cache" class="tab-title">More cache</h4><p>With the Wii (and GameCube), Broadway/Gekko only disposed of 256 KB of L2 cache and 64 KB of L1 cache. With the Wii U, L1 cache stays the same with each core of Espresso, but two of them are now provided with <strong>512 KB of L2 cache</strong> and the third’s got a whopping <strong>2 MB of L2</strong>. In reality, this doesn’t mean there’s 2.5 MB of ‘practical’ cache, as different cores may need to cache the same portion from RAM, something that wouldn’t happen if cache <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/xbox-360/#shared-cache">were shared</a> (but then, other problems would arise!).</p><p>All L2 caches found in Espresso are <strong>4-way associative</strong>. Compare this to the 8-way associations in Xenon and Cell, which in the case of Xenon, was meant to alleviate the 3 cores competing for 1 MB of shared L2. With Espresso, iterating through cache associations will take less time, but there will be more frequent cache misses.</p><p>To handle cache coherency between the three independent L2 cache blocks, Espresso’s internal Bus Interface abides by the <strong>MERSI</strong> protocol (same as Cell/Xenon). For reference, Broadway (a single-core system) used the MEI protocol.</p><p>As a side note, L2 memory in Espresso is of type <strong>eDRAM</strong>, as opposed to SRAM. Furthermore, the L1 block still offers locked and RAM-to-L1 DMA instructions (<a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/gamecube/#ibms-enhancements">as the GameCube’s CPU did</a>).</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-1-2-a-recallable-bus">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-1-4-room-for-improvement">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-1-4-room-for-improvement"><h4 id="tab-1-4-room-for-improvement" class="tab-title">Room for improvement</h4><p>As emphasised by fail0verflow, the Wii U, as a system, is in fact <strong>not cache coherent</strong>. External I/O can alter memory without the awareness of Espresso, therefore cache is not automatically refreshed in those situations. By contrast, the Xbox 360’s <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/xbox-360/#clever-l2-access">Southbridge</a> notifies the caches after peripherals DMA to main RAM.</p><p>Moreover, two existing PowerPC instructions made for multi-processing environments, <code>lwarx</code> (Load Word and Reserve Indexed) and <code>stwcx</code> (Store Word Conditional Indexed), no longer function as intended. As fail0verflow also noted <sup id="bibref:11"><a href="#bib:graphics-smp" role="doc-biblioref">[11]</a></sup>, these now need a manual cache flush to work as intended. At least it’s not the first PowerPC variant to ship with broken instructions (see <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/xbox-360/#a-new-but-short-lived-instruction">Xbox 360’s xdcbt</a>).</p><p>It’s not all bad news, luckily. At least Espresso inherits Gekko’s ability for <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/gamecube/#the-powerpc-gekko">out-of-order instruction execution</a>, something that had to be <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/xbox-360/#revisiting-old-paradigms">cut from Xenon and Cell</a>.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-1-3-more-cache">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next pre">Next »</a></div></div></div></div><h3 id="memory-available">Memory Available</h3><p>This section is simple and complicated at the same time. In summary, there are three places to store volatile data:</p><ul><li>A hefty chunk of <strong>2 GB of DDR3 SDRAM</strong> called <strong>MEM2</strong>.</li><li>A smaller block of <strong>32 MB of EDRAM</strong> named <strong>MEM1</strong>.</li><li>An even smaller piece of <strong>3 MB of <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/gamecube/#clever-memory-system">1T-SRAM</a></strong> called <strong>MEM0</strong>.</li></ul><p>The reason for such disparity is that you may remember MEM1 and MEM0 from the times of the Wii and GameCube. They’ve been carried forward with the Wii U, albeit with a slight increase of MEM1.</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/espresso/memory.22ea5058d7827b7946e23361bf0ce849a33f23a394f71c629d708e08076c99a9.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="945" height="452" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/espresso/memory.22ea5058d7827b7946e23361bf0ce849a33f23a394f71c629d708e08076c99a9.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Memory layout of general-purpose memory (in ‘Wii U’ mode).</figcaption></figure><p>In any case, from the developer’s point of view, only MEM2 and MEM1 (the two bigger blocks) are accessible. The 2 GB of DDR3 may hold any kind of data (supplying both CPU and GPU), while the other two have more limited functions. MEM1 is used for graphics data (more details in the ‘Graphics’ section) and MEM0 is used by the operating system (more details in the ‘Operating System’ section).</p><p>In some ways, this system follows the Unified Memory architecture (UMA). Though, with MEM1 and MEM2 in the middle, I wouldn’t say this system is fully compliant with the UMA model (unlike some of its competitors).</p><h4 id="gddr3-or-ddr3">GDDR3 or DDR3?</h4><p>The old Wii employed GDDR3 memory, which is particularly fast for graphics operations. The Wii U’s choice is not only larger but also features a new type called <strong>DDR3</strong> (without the ‘G’ at the start). Does this mean the Wii U has been downgraded? Confusingly enough, no.</p><p>GDDR3 memory is an improved version of DDR2 for graphics-related functions. Years later saw the arrival of DDR3, which succeeds both DDR2 and GDDR3. Have I lost you already? Well, to make matters more baffling, the follow-up GDDR4 and GDDR5 are enhancements over DDR3 and no other.</p><p>The nomenclature is unnecessarily deceptive. But let’s not lose our focus, the Wii U employs DDR3 and that means higher bandwidth compared to the Wii’s GDDR3.</p><h3 id="becoming-a-wii">Becoming a Wii</h3><p>I’m eager to say that, while the new hardware may look underwhelming in some areas, the logic behind Wii backwards compatibility reaches the same level of dedication as the Nintendo DS or Game Boy Advance.</p><p>The methodology applied shares the same principles of those two consoles as well. Instead of resorting to <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/xbox-360/#backwards-compatibility">software emulation</a> or <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation-3/#backwards-compatibility">provisional hardware</a>, <strong>the Wii U has been built as a superset of the Wii</strong>. Thus, it can easily replicate the hardware of the Wii by just hiding its modern features.</p><p>Having said that, whenever the Wii U decides to ‘become a Wii’, Espresso deactivates two of its cores (leaving a single Broadway core) and MEM2 hides 1984 MB of RAM (leaving the previous amount of 64 MB). Once in ‘Virtual Wii’ (<strong>vWii</strong>) mode, the old Wii game can safely assume it’s running on top of a real Wii.</p><p>There are more nooks and crannies behind this compatibility mode involving <em>obscure</em> I/O (explained in due time), so keep on reading if you are curious about this process!</p><h3 id="the-last-venture-of-powerpc">The last venture of PowerPC</h3><p>As we reach the end of the CPU section, it looks like this will be my last analysis of a PowerPC-based system (at least chronologically, I haven’t talked about the Apple Pippin yet).</p><p>The PowerPC has been an interesting development, with its ups and downs. And while it didn’t manage to dethrone x86, it did conquer three generations of consoles.</p><p>In any case, <em>our beloved</em> Espresso is, at its essence, a modern improvement to a fundamentally outdated platform. Both IBM and Motorola already dismissed the 750CL line in favour of the 7400 and the 970 lines, respectively. Yet, it’s curious to see how IBM had to dig up their old designs to produce a console that could compete in the 2010s. I guess the lack of a consumer version of Espresso is proof that IBM wasn’t interested in pushing Espresso any further.</p><p>But hey, just like with Xenon or Cell, it’s all part of an evolutionary line. I don’t believe these kinds of technologies are forgotten or abandoned, but their designs and expertise eventually merge into other projects.</p><hr><h2 id="graphics">Graphics</h2><p>So while the CPU can be considered a <em>tribute</em> to legacy technologies, let me tell you that the GPU is <em>officially</em> part of the next generation.</p><figure class="tabs nested centered-container"><ul class="tab-links nested"><li id="nestedtab-1-1-mario-3d-link" class="active"><a href="#nestedtab-1-1-mario-3d">Mario 3D</a></li><li id="nestedtab-1-2-hyrule-link"><a href="#nestedtab-1-2-hyrule">Hyrule</a></li><li id="nestedtab-1-3-pikmin-link"><a href="#nestedtab-1-3-pikmin">Pikmin</a></li><li id="nestedtab-1-4-splatoon-link"><a href="#nestedtab-1-4-splatoon">Splatoon</a></li><li id="nestedtab-1-5-zelda-link"><a href="#nestedtab-1-5-zelda">Zelda</a></li></ul><figure class="tab active nested" id="nestedtab-1-1-mario-3d"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/screenshots/mario3d.c881d1bd1b6ed8aea0170c2455b1b14769084737f05a3c292ece99a8459d7a70.jpg"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/screenshots/mario3d.c881d1bd1b6ed8aea0170c2455b1b14769084737f05a3c292ece99a8459d7a70_hu_e6f845767002cf74.webp 500w,

All are rendered at their maximum resolution (1280x720 pixels) except for Wind Waker.</figcaption></figure><p>The graphics logic is found within a big silicon chip sitting next to Espresso, it’s called <strong>Latte</strong>, operates at <strong>550 MHz</strong> <sup id="bibref:12"><a href="#bib:graphics-speed" role="doc-biblioref">[12]</a></sup> and, to make a long story short, it’s broad and complex. Latte houses a lot more infrastructure than just graphics, so don’t worry as the former will be explained in the next sections of the article. For now, just remember that the graphics block lives in Latte.</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/motherboard/soc.38a8a1efada68b5df61254c204caac8a6b6705512b93c3fc7165a64a4e9f4da8.jpg"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/motherboard/soc.38a8a1efada68b5df61254c204caac8a6b6705512b93c3fc7165a64a4e9f4da8_hu_dca2e17023dfdb89.webp 500w,

https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/motherboard/soc.38a8a1efada68b5df61254c204caac8a6b6705512b93c3fc7165a64a4e9f4da8_hu_16103444ab0cc93e.webp 1000w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="1000" height="781" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/motherboard/soc.38a8a1efada68b5df61254c204caac8a6b6705512b93c3fc7165a64a4e9f4da8.jpg" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">The SoC photo again. So you can <em>contemplate</em> it after being made aware of Latte.</figcaption></figure><p>By the way, for the Italian readers, as you may know, the Wii U’s codenames are made of terminology related to coffee, and ‘Latte’ is no exception because that’s what non-Italians refer to ‘Latte macchiato’ :’)</p><h3 id="old-partnerships-with-new-challenges">Old partnerships with new challenges</h3><p>Homologous to Nintendo’s good relationship with IBM, the company also maintained a unique partnership they started all the way back with the Nintendo 64.</p><p>ArtX was the group known for designing the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/nintendo-64/#graphics">Reality Coprocessor</a> (then as part of Silicon Graphics) which then went on to invent <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/gamecube/#graphics">Flipper</a>, the GameCube’s unique SoC that houses its signature graphics processor. Years later, after being acquired by ‘ATI’, they supplied <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/wii/#graphics">Hollywood</a> for the Wii, from which we find a sped-up version of Flipper’s GPU. But most importantly and around the same time, ATI had been working on a cutting-edge invention for Microsoft. The result was <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/xbox-360/#graphics">Xenos</a> and <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/xbox-360/#a-new-foundation-on-the-way">its new shader model</a> for the masses.</p><p>Years after the release of the Xbox 360, ATI got acquired by a silicon company named ‘AMD’, which brings us to explain a bit of AMD history…</p><h4 id="titans-in-the-ring">Titans in the ring</h4><p>Initially known as the sidekick of Intel, AMD used to be the second supplier of Intel’s CPUs (i.e. 8086 and 80286), although this relationship broke down as soon as AMD started selling an unauthorised version of the 80386 that, to Intel’s dismay, improved upon the original designs of the chip <sup id="bibref:13"><a href="#bib:cpu-am386" role="doc-biblioref">[13]</a></sup>. This didn’t sit well with Intel and, soon enough, the two became head-to-head competitors.</p><p>Such was the competition, that in the late 90s, Intel’s plans to captivate the 64-bit market with their new line of ‘Itanium’ CPUs were soon thwarted by AMD’s simpler alternative: an extension of x86 called ‘amd64’ (also referred to as ‘x86-64’). Thus, Intel was forced to adopt AMD’s standard instead. For reference, amd64 still serves as the ISA of current x86 CPUs (as of 2022).</p><p>It’s never been all jolly for AMD, however. As the pressure from competing with Intel also brought a share of flops out of them (i.e. the abandoned “3DNow!” extension, the delay of Fusion, etc) and now, with the acquisition of ATI in 2006, AMD found itself facing two fronts: Intel in the CPU market and Nvidia on the graphics side.</p><h4 id="the-next-radeon">The next Radeon</h4><p>Now that we’ve positioned AMD on the map, let’s analyse the state of ATI’s Radeon line.</p><p>After the introduction of Xenos and its new architecture based on the ‘unified shaders’ model, ATI was still too busy with Microsoft’s project so they couldn’t allocate enough resources to bring Xenos to the PC market in the short term. Thus, the remaining teams focused on maintaining their classical x1000/R500 series, which left enough gap for Nvidia to ship their unified card named <strong>GeForce 8</strong> (featuring the <strong>Tesla</strong> architecture) before ATI. Finally, in 2007 (two years after Xenos), ATI presented the <strong>Radeon 2000</strong> series (codenamed <strong>R600</strong>) and its <strong>TeraScale</strong> architecture. The new design, now free of Microsoft’s budget and licensing control, brought all the advancements of Xenos along with optional extras for those users who were willing to pay the premium pricing.</p><p>Now, for the Wii U, ATI prepared a Terascale-based card for Nintendo, but it’s never been officially confirmed which model they based it on. Fail0verflow relates it to the Radeon HD 4000 series (codenamed <strong>R700</strong>) <sup id="bibref:14"><a href="#bib:cpu-fail0verflow" role="doc-biblioref">[14]</a></sup>. For reference, R700-based cards launched in 2008 and were an incremental update to the R670 and R600 series. The most apparent changes are the inclusion of faster video decoding hardware and support for OpenCL, though only the former will be usable (to some degree) on the Wii U.</p><p>In any case, the Wii U’s GPU goes by two names, Nintendo calls it <strong>GPU7</strong> when referring to the hardware and <strong>GX2</strong> when referring to the API. For this article, I’ll use the term ‘GPU7’ as I’ll be focusing on the physical capabilities.</p><h3 id="architecture-of-gpu7">Architecture of GPU7</h3><p>The TeraScale architecture is the materialisation of Xenos/Crayola ported to the PC market… and GPU7 is TeraScale brought back to a console. Its most identifiable trait is the use of a <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/xbox-360/#a-new-foundation-on-the-way">unified shader model</a> that centralises both vertex and pixel units into a single block, now called <strong>SIMD unit</strong>.</p><p>It’s worth emphasising that when Xenos arrived, the API model was still based on the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/xbox/#graphics">segregated shader model</a>, so the libraries didn’t provide additional functionality that was now possible with a consolidated compute unit. Well, thanks to the subsequent updates (Direct3D 10 and OpenGL 3.3), that’s not the case anymore. Back to the Wii U, GX2 is the only API available and it’s based on <strong>OpenGL 3.3</strong>.</p><h4 id="organising-the-content">Organising the content</h4><p>Most of the content related to graphics resides in the aforementioned <strong>2 GB of DDR3 RAM</strong> called <strong>MEM2</strong>, which is shared between the CPU and GPU. That means the GPU must place its materials there, but MEM2 is relatively slow and not prepared for the contention that concurrent CPU and GPU work leads to. Therefore, Nintendo implemented something <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/xbox-360/#organising-the-content">similar to the Xbox 360</a>, and that is the inclusion of a dedicated and closer <strong>32 MB of EDRAM</strong> (called <strong>MEM1</strong>) for fast operations (i.e. render targets and other high-demanded buffers). Consequently, not only large frames may be rendered, but also have extra space to perform post-processing (i.e. anti-aliasing) with acceptable performance.</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/gpu/gpu_content.29a4b22afb8007942eafd00be46fcf427edf15eaf2ede97de3c3075fbd4cf2ff.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="836" height="620" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/gpu/gpu_content.29a4b22afb8007942eafd00be46fcf427edf15eaf2ede97de3c3075fbd4cf2ff.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Example of how data is organised across the memory available.</figcaption></figure><p>Conversely, the Wii U’s EDRAM is larger than the Xbox 360’s (meaning the need for <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/dreamcast/#graphics">tiling</a> is reduced). However, it does not include <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/xbox-360/#tab-2-5-pixel-operations">dedicated circuitry for post-processing</a>.</p><h3 id="constructing-the-frame">Constructing the frame</h3><p>This is the signature section of the Architecture of Consoles series where I attempt to explain the process of converting the geometry (coming from the CPU) into pixels (which users eventually see on the telly). Nevertheless, in this article, the explanations will be a bit different as the fundamentals of TeraScale were already explained in the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/xbox-360/#overview">Xbox 360 article</a>.</p><p>The most important changes since Xenos is the implementation (or better said, standardisation) of <strong>Geometry Shaders</strong> and <strong>Compute Shaders</strong>, both of which take advantage of the new capabilities of the unified shaders. This doesn’t mean GPU7 had to be completely re-designed to make way for these two stages, what happened is that APIs had been expanded to enable new applications without considerably changing the existing circuitry.</p><p>Being an AMD/ATI chip built for a Nintendo console, GX2 supports two shader APIs, <strong>OpenGL’s GLSL 3.3</strong> and <strong>OpenGL ESSL</strong>. The SDK also comes with some extensions to provide functionality only available on GPU7, but it doesn’t support OpenCL and certainly not Direct3D.</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/gpu/gpu_pipeline.6cb422ec7fcce8e04e1401e22f2ef108f9d6d664e4cc54b251e7eb9ef03bd490.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="548" height="479" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/gpu/gpu_pipeline.6cb422ec7fcce8e04e1401e22f2ef108f9d6d664e4cc54b251e7eb9ef03bd490.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Overview of the graphics pipeline in GPU7.</figcaption></figure><p>Be as it may, GPU7 still inherits the designs of the Radeon R700 series, so GPU7’s pipeline is somewhat aligned to Direct3D 10.1 and OpenGL 3.3 standards. Although, their respective shader languages aren’t natively understood by GPU7 (they require proprietary compilers shipped with the official SDK).</p><p>As a side note, typical Radeon cards for the PC market use AGP or PCI-e bus interfaces. Well, the Wii U hardware still relies on the old-school practice of exposing I/O registers as memory locations <sup id="bibref:15"><a href="#bib:graphics-mmio" role="doc-biblioref">[15]</a></sup>. I guess neither Nintendo nor AMD were concerned as this is all part of a custom design.</p><p>Let’s now go over the pipeline, stage by stage. Since the design is very similar to the Xbox 360’s <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/xbox-360/#graphics">Xenos GPU</a>, I’ll try to focus on the novelties of GPU7 instead to avoid repeating information.</p><div class="tabs"><ul class="tab-links"><li id="tab-2-1-commands-link" class="active"><a href="#tab-2-1-commands">Commands</a></li><li id="tab-2-2-vertex-link"><a href="#tab-2-2-vertex">Vertex</a></li><li id="tab-2-3-geometry-link"><a href="#tab-2-3-geometry">Geometry</a></li><li id="tab-2-4-rasteriser-link"><a href="#tab-2-4-rasteriser">Rasteriser</a></li><li id="tab-2-5-fragment-link"><a href="#tab-2-5-fragment">Fragment</a></li><li id="tab-2-6-pixel-operations-link"><a href="#tab-2-6-pixel-operations">Pixel Operations</a></li></ul><div class="tab-content"><div class="tab active body-side" id="tab-2-1-commands"><h4 id="tab-2-1-commands" class="tab-title">Commands</h4><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/gpu/gpu_pipeline_commands.603535a3783d776207fbb52b7e805943e7cf2bb835064e4d3b533057c5485e03.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="548" height="390" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/gpu/gpu_pipeline_commands.603535a3783d776207fbb52b7e805943e7cf2bb835064e4d3b533057c5485e03.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Overview of the command stage.</figcaption></figure><p>With most graphics cards, especially ATI/AMD ones, the starting point is always the <strong>Command Processor</strong> <sup id="bibref:16"><a href="#bib:graphics-r700isa" role="doc-biblioref">[16]</a></sup>. As we’ve seen many times before, this is the door between the GPU and the outside world (i.e. the CPU).</p><p>In the case of the GPU7, the Command Processor reads commands stored in RAM and activates the necessary engines within the chip. Most notably, GPU7 features a dedicated <strong>Direct Memory Access</strong> (DMA) controller to manipulate data between MEM1 and MEM2 without the intervention of the CPU.</p><p>Furthermore, DMA may work asynchronously (out of pace with the rest of the circuitry), so GPU7 provides a few commands to refresh its cache and synchronise with DMA (in the form of a semaphore) to maintain order.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev pre">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-2-2-vertex">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-2-2-vertex"><h4 id="tab-2-2-vertex" class="tab-title">Vertex</h4><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/gpu/pipeline_vertex.d7f571fa994400299656c1880923bcc139fc2ea515b9c22bda5f925ca691ee66.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="782" height="600" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/gpu/pipeline_vertex.d7f571fa994400299656c1880923bcc139fc2ea515b9c22bda5f925ca691ee66.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Overview of the vertex stage. You’ll soon find that this stage and the pixel stage are not <em>that</em> different.</figcaption></figure><p>At first glance, this stage is pretty much in line with Xenos/Crayola except that some blocks have been expanded (increased cache) while others have contracted (reduced number of ALU units and the Memory Export path is shorter). None of this necessarily means a performance decrease, however, as let’s not forget GPU7 is ~7 years ahead of Xenos.</p><p>To start with, let’s take a look at the ALUs. Xenos resorted to three shader pipes (blocks of 16 ALUs) to execute the vertex shaders. GPU7 only bundles two blocks of 16 ALUs, but each block is now wrapped around a larger circuitry named <strong>SIMD processor</strong>, which I assume denotes the addition of larger circuitry (dedicated <strong>8 KB of L1 cache</strong>, plus the extra interfaces and control units) to sustain more concurrent traffic. Furthermore, each ALU is made of four ‘sub-ALUs’, allowing the former to compute <strong>vectors made of four scalars</strong> at once. ATI/AMD calls these sub-ALUs <strong>stream processors</strong> and it’s a common marketing term.</p><p>Now, instead of the Sequencer dispatching the calculations right away as they come, they are first combined into a larger batch of <strong>64 vertices</strong> along with some meta-data to control the operation <sup id="bibref:17"><a href="#bib:graphics-r7xxacceleration" role="doc-biblioref">[17]</a></sup>, this is called a <strong>Wavefront</strong>. The batch is then sent to the two SIMDs and, considering the fact there’re only 32 ALUs in GPU7, they take <strong>four cycles</strong> to be computed.</p><p>I assume this new design is what enables manufacturers to devise different ranges of graphics cards, with the most expensive including more SIMD units (thus taking fewer clock cycles to complete). As game consoles are not particularly famous for embedding high-end hardware (instead, they compensate by being more efficient), four clock cycles are what it takes in the Wii U to process a Wavefront.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-2-1-commands">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-2-3-geometry">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-2-3-geometry"><h4 id="tab-2-3-geometry" class="tab-title">Geometry</h4><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/gpu/pipeline_geometry.97e07d33bb01a8025354188d444984d77020e4172f267461cfbf5df735c9d450.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="726" height="452" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/gpu/pipeline_geometry.97e07d33bb01a8025354188d444984d77020e4172f267461cfbf5df735c9d450.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Overview of the geometry stage.</figcaption></figure><p>The geometry shader is a new stage of the graphics pipeline that appeared right after the two famous APIs (Direct3D and OpenGL) incorporated the unified shader into their specification. The purpose of this new stage is to allow developers to manipulate primitives (points, lines or triangles) as opposed to single vertices <sup id="bibref:18"><a href="#bib:graphics-geometryshader" role="doc-biblioref">[18]</a></sup>. This can be useful for <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation-2/#infinite-worlds">procedurally generating</a> new geometry out of existing one (i.e. devise shadows, fur and so forth). The GPU7, like the Radeon R700, inherits compliance with OpenGL 3.3 and therefore supports this new shader type.</p><p>Behind the scenes, however, the geometry stage is just another ‘mode’ of the vertex stage. To make a long story short, if geometry shaders are activated, the vertex stage doesn’t forward the data for rasterisation right away. Instead, the outputted data is saved into a dedicated buffer in MEM2 and the vertex stage starts over but fetches data from the geometry buffer. Then, Wavefronts are assembled to grab the indices of up to 64 primitives along with meta-data denoting a geometry shader will be executed. Afterwards, the Sequencer reads the new Wavefront, parses the primitives and sends them to the two SIMDs for computing. The process is repeated until all primitives are processed.</p><p>Finally, the pipeline continues to the rasterisation stage.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-2-2-vertex">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-2-4-rasteriser">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-2-4-rasteriser"><h4 id="tab-2-4-rasteriser" class="tab-title">Rasteriser</h4><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/gpu/pipeline_raster.28b809042dab40af2f4e92cdfd970ddd701bc0ceca27bb3a704f3d3c3083b3aa.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="833" height="345" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/gpu/pipeline_raster.28b809042dab40af2f4e92cdfd970ddd701bc0ceca27bb3a704f3d3c3083b3aa.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Overview of the rasteriser stage.</figcaption></figure><p>The rasterisation stage tends to be much simpler than other stages. The main reason being the act of converting vertices into pixels is mostly systematic, and no extra programmability is needed (aside from a few parameters available to tweak). As such, this stage is identical to Crayola/Xenos.</p><p>Be as it may, the Z and stencil buffers are not allocated on dedicated memory anymore. Instead, the new <strong>Render backend</strong> block (performing Z and stencil testing, with support for <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/xbox-360/#tab-2-3-rasterisation">hierarchical testing</a> as well) must access RAM to work (either EDRAM or main RAM).</p><p>The rasteriser can compose frames of up to 8192 x 8192 pixels using 128-bit pixel formats <sup id="bibref:19"><a href="#bib:graphics-r7xxreference" role="doc-biblioref">[19]</a></sup>. This would allow massive frames with HDR colour quality. However and for obvious reasons, developers don’t need frames <em>that</em> big (1280 x 720 will suffice for this console), except HDR which will be used thoroughly.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-2-3-geometry">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-2-5-fragment">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-2-5-fragment"><h4 id="tab-2-5-fragment" class="tab-title">Fragment</h4><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/gpu/pipeline_pixel.ba26aab81b8093591f509c218c8b1417efd616a354bb0241cfc34979115636e3.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="785" height="480" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/gpu/pipeline_pixel.ba26aab81b8093591f509c218c8b1417efd616a354bb0241cfc34979115636e3.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Overview of the Pixel/Fragment Shader stage.</figcaption></figure><p>The pixel shader stage follows the same methodology as the vertex shader except it’s now pixels being shuffled around. After going through Xenos’ pixel capabilities and GPU7’s new vertex pipeline, I’m afraid there’s not a lot left to explain here.</p><p>The block that fetches textures to the SIMD units is now called <strong>Texture Pipe</strong> and there’re two of them. Each contains <strong>8 KB of L1 cache</strong> and they both share <strong>32 KB of L2 cache</strong> when accessing RAM. Additionally, they can perform up to 16x Anisotropic filtering on the spot and can also fetch cube maps (used for environmental mapping/reflections).</p><p>I guess it’s worth pointing out that the shader model (OpenGL GLSL 3.3) adds an abundance of new routines (i.e. new types of texture blending, bitwise operators, texture swizzling) for manipulating textures and removes many constraints (such as the number of instructions allowed per shader). All of which makes the life of developers a bit easier.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-2-4-rasteriser">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-2-6-pixel-operations">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-2-6-pixel-operations"><h4 id="tab-2-6-pixel-operations" class="tab-title">Pixel Operations</h4><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/gpu/pipeline_post.06c52712016fa40ea8911712b4a71136a4aaa36bdabe8c2ebc40328f424dec72.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="696" height="407" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/gpu/pipeline_post.06c52712016fa40ea8911712b4a71136a4aaa36bdabe8c2ebc40328f424dec72.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Overview of pixel operations available.</figcaption></figure><p>Once the frame has been rendered, developers can apply more Z-testing (in case it wasn’t activated at an earlier stage), colour blending and, finally, export the pixels to the frame-buffer for display. This is all performed by the <strong>Render backends</strong> (there’s of two of them) which are found at the end of the Pixel shader stage.</p><p>Finally, even though the Wii U doesn’t feature the sophisticated circuitry that the Xbox 360 bundles within its EDRAM module, there are still many interesting capabilities provided by GPU7. This includes automatic Multisample Anti-aliasing of up to 16 passes (<strong>MSAA 16x</strong>) to soften edges, which surprisingly doesn’t require <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/xbox-360/#tab-2-5-pixel-operations">tiled rendering</a> since the larger 32 MB of EDRAM (MEM1) of the Wii U is more than enough for these operations (well, maybe MSAA 16x will eat up too much MEM1, however, MSAA 8x is still acceptable).</p><p>Apart from that, we have to take into account the custom algorithms programmers may decide to implement. This is thanks to the flexibility of the APIs and the vast amount of shader operations available, including <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/xbox-360/#the-impact-on-the-industry">Compute Shaders</a> (which offload CPU computations into the GPU).</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-2-5-fragment">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next pre">Next »</a></div></div></div></div><h3 id="interactive-comparison">Interactive comparison</h3><p>I’ve added new 3D models on the interactive viewer so you can check
