and bones, especially on the hands and face, which make the model react more realistically to ambient effects and animations. In doing so, scenes look more natural throughout gameplay.</p><h3 id="video-decoding">Video decoding</h3><p>An additional feature beyond the 3D rendering capabilities of GPU7 is the inclusion of <strong>H.264 decoding circuitry</strong> that transforms streams of H.264-compressed data into raw frames that the GPU can understand (and subsequently render on the screen). The main advantage being bandwidth efficiency without performance penalties.</p><p>Consequently, the H.264 block is used for displaying motion video on the game in any way the developer prefers (i.e. within gameplay or as a cinematic).</p><h3 id="video-output">Video Output</h3><p>Time has come for Nintendo to ditch their proprietary analogue circuitry and embrace (at least one!) video standard. Lo and behold, an <strong>HDMI 1.4</strong> socket is finally included on the back, along with the traditional <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/wii/#video-signal">AV Multi Out</a> as a ‘backup’.</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/back.475a7ca6b8501d409881014b87df0313e1ac119d3a583f8465b79f2fbf5d2b43.jpg"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/back.475a7ca6b8501d409881014b87df0313e1ac119d3a583f8465b79f2fbf5d2b43_hu_7782dcc66146f251.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/back.475a7ca6b8501d409881014b87df0313e1ac119d3a583f8465b79f2fbf5d2b43_hu_64a38de930b98d2.webp 800w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/back.475a7ca6b8501d409881014b87df0313e1ac119d3a583f8465b79f2fbf5d2b43_hu_3e8ecb5fe932be51.webp 1000w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="1000" height="455" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/back.475a7ca6b8501d409881014b87df0313e1ac119d3a583f8465b79f2fbf5d2b43.jpg" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Back view of the console, showing both video options (HDMI and Multi AV).</figcaption></figure><p>Now, even though the output resolution can go as high as 1080p, most games resort to <strong>720p</strong> to balance game performance with the use of anti-aliasing and a large resolution. Using 720p also helps developers to keep support for 480i and 576i without altering the game logic (as the video encoder takes care of automatically downscaling the frame). This modus operandi matches the one of the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation-3/#a-unified-video-output">PlayStation 3</a> and the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/xbox-360/#new-attitudes-towards-resolutions">Xbox 360</a>.</p><h3 id="a-secondary-gpu">A secondary GPU</h3><p>With all being said, how come this console can still play Wii games? Is there some sort of GPU7-to-Hollywood emulator running behind the scenes? Well, the short answer is <strong>no</strong>. It may surprise you Nintendo went straight ahead and added the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/wii/#graphics">old GPU circuit from Hollywood</a> (let’s call it ‘Wii GPU’) inside Latte as well <sup id="bibref:20"><a href="#bib:cpu-fail0verflow" role="doc-biblioref">[20]</a></sup>. This block only works when a Wii game is running. Although, the Wii GPU houses the old <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/gamecube/#clever-memory-system">3 MB of 1T-SRAM</a> which is the one we now know as <strong>MEM0</strong>. So, at least the extra memory is used by the new hardware.</p><p>Furthermore, Nintendo also fitted an extra chip called <strong>DMCU</strong> to replicate the old <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/gamecube/#internal-io">Video Interface</a>. According to fail0verflow, the DMCU is just a <strong>Motorola 68HC11</strong> controller programmed to behave like the precursor. Its only purpose is to receive commands from Wii games and forward the frame to GPU7, so the latter can broadcast it to the TV. Due to the fact Wii games are made for PAL/NTSC screens, the GPU7’s video encoder must upscale it (which, in my experience, is not very good at doing so…).</p><p>If you wonder, there’s no ‘Wii GPU and GPU7’ co-processing available for Wii U games. It would’ve been ‘interesting’ though, albeit knowing one would bottleneck the other…</p><hr><h2 id="audio">Audio</h2><p>At first, I had assumed the Wii U implemented its audio functions through software (like its competitors <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation-3/#audio">started doing</a>). But then, other questions arose: How is the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/wii/#audio">complex DSP</a> of the Wii emulated? Is Espresso powerful enough?</p><p>Well, that’s not all. Unlike the Wii, the audio pipeline of the Wii U must service three endpoints:</p><ul><li>The <strong>Television</strong>, expecting up to 6 channels (typically only 2/stereo).</li><li>The <strong>GamePad</strong> with up to 4 channels (a.k.a surround audio).</li><li>Up to four <strong>Wii Remotes</strong> (with one <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/wii/#next-gen-controllers">low-quality</a> channel each).</li></ul><p>Lo and behold, <strong>Latte also houses a custom DSP</strong> that performs audio synthesis. It’s operated through Nintendo’s libraries, although developers can extend the audio pipeline through software (at the cost of CPU cycles) if it’s not enough for them.</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/audio.8338b436daa23f7c171e2f1015da9cf85ea1d5e03ddd9d266530bbfefde0fca6.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="710" height="362" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/audio.8338b436daa23f7c171e2f1015da9cf85ea1d5e03ddd9d266530bbfefde0fca6.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Overview of the audio pipeline. In this example, the game is loaded from the disc drive.</figcaption></figure><p>The DSP helps with mixing and sequencing tasks, the rest (i.e. filtering, effects, etc) is done with software (part of Espresso’s workload). Moreover, Nintendo’s libraries take care of workload management, where audio tasks are first assigned to the DSP and, in the event of full capacity, these are sent to Espresso.</p><p>The amount of workload and the resulting performance will depend on many factors, including the type of encoding streamed (i.e. ADPCM takes up more resources than PCM). Programmers must first test their code using the audio profiling tools provided to come up with an efficient implementation.</p><hr><h2 id="io">I/O</h2><p>When it comes to I/O and interaction methods, Nintendo still manages to break the status quo. From the hardware perspective, the choices and internal organisation of these components tend to reach cost-effectiveness at obsessive levels. It may be because this area is under the complete direction of Nintendo’s engineers, and they strive for keeping the console at an affordable price.</p><h3 id="a-familiar-arm-chip">A familiar ARM chip</h3><p>Remember the old <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/wii/#the-hidden-co-processor">ARM926EJ-S</a> that had <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/wii/#the-fall-of-encryption">complete control over the Wii’s hardware</a>? Well, <strong>the same CPU is found in the Wii U</strong>. The main difference, however, is that Starlet is now surrounded by larger amounts of memory (<strong>96 KB of SRAM</strong>) and implements better algorithms for security-related tasks.</p><p>By the way, in the absence of an official name for the ARM9 CPU in the Wii U (after all, in the eyes of Nintendo, you shouldn’t know about this chip…), fail0verflow came up with their identifier: <strong>Starbuck</strong>.</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/_diagrams/main.f7826e09f39fc4f0a6d96aea1689966b95bfc0c0bad9cb37716cf4be9f82efef.png"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/_diagrams/main.f7826e09f39fc4f0a6d96aea1689966b95bfc0c0bad9cb37716cf4be9f82efef_hu_f57b3c69175407ba.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/_diagrams/main.f7826e09f39fc4f0a6d96aea1689966b95bfc0c0bad9cb37716cf4be9f82efef_hu_b79f259a841e9ac7.webp 800w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/_diagrams/main.f7826e09f39fc4f0a6d96aea1689966b95bfc0c0bad9cb37716cf4be9f82efef_hu_e85a273907fcfd33.webp 1715w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="1715" height="1130" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/_diagrams/main.f7826e09f39fc4f0a6d96aea1689966b95bfc0c0bad9cb37716cf4be9f82efef.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Main diagram of the console’s architecture. Notice how Starbuck is located in a strategic area within Latte.</figcaption></figure><p>That being said, Starbuck’s program has been greatly enhanced. I go over it in the ‘Operating System’ and ‘Anti-Piracy and Homebrew’ sections. For now, just remember Starbuck is the equivalent of the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/xbox/#motherboard-architecture">Southbridge</a>.</p><h3 id="external-interfaces">External interfaces</h3><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/front.c7216218d67390fb870ce85b4d6208c82c0e78396beeb0802146819e84b3e31c.jpg"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/front.c7216218d67390fb870ce85b4d6208c82c0e78396beeb0802146819e84b3e31c_hu_4f9efd766400db6a.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/front.c7216218d67390fb870ce85b4d6208c82c0e78396beeb0802146819e84b3e31c_hu_e3a50513b0559e8.webp 800w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/front.c7216218d67390fb870ce85b4d6208c82c0e78396beeb0802146819e84b3e31c_hu_efba32dbb45a5071.webp 1000w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="1000" height="436" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/front.c7216218d67390fb870ce85b4d6208c82c0e78396beeb0802146819e84b3e31c.jpg" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Front view of the console with the faceplate door opened.</figcaption></figure><p>Looking at this console from the outside, the Wii U offers the following interfaces:</p><ul><li>Four <strong>USB 2.0</strong> ports to connect accessories or mass storage devices. Two of them are at the back and the others at the front.</li><li>An <strong>SDHC card slot</strong> for storage.</li><li>A proprietary <strong>Sensor bar port</strong> to plug the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/wii/#next-gen-controllers">Sensor bar</a>, enabling up to four <strong>Wii Remotes</strong> to control the Wii U (in addition to the GamePad). Remember the sensor bar is just four ‘dumb’ LEDs beaming infrared light, the real magic happens inside the Wii Remote!</li></ul><h3 id="internal-interfaces">Internal interfaces</h3><p>As mentioned before, Starbuck is connected to the majority (if not all) of the I/O peripherals. Considering its strong backwards compatibility with the Wii and the inclusion of the same ARM9 core for I/O processing, I assume Starbuck still relies on <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/wii/#the-hidden-co-processor">AMBA buses</a> to communicate with its peripherals, specifically the <strong>AHB type</strong> (since the new interfaces require higher amounts of bandwidth).</p><p>Having said that, Starbuck is connected to the following endpoints:</p><ul><li>The <strong>NAND Interface</strong> pointing to <strong>1 GB of NAND</strong> storage. In practice, only half is used by the Wii U system and the other is reserved for backwards compatibility (the old Wii storage).</li><li>Three <strong>SD Host Controllers</strong>, each providing access to:<ul><li>The separate <strong>Broadcom BCM43362</strong> chip, for Wi-Fi connectivity (2.4 GHz 802.11 b/g/n).</li><li>The <strong>SDHC card slot</strong>.</li><li>Either <strong>8 GB or 32 GB worth of eMMC storage</strong> for storing user data.</li></ul></li><li>Three <strong>USB 2.0 Host Controllers</strong>, each giving access to:<ul><li>The separate <strong>Bluetooth 4.0 module</strong> that wirelessly interacts with the Wii Remotes and the ‘Pro’ controller (all of them are optional).</li><li>The aforementioned <strong>four USB ports</strong>.</li><li>Another separate chip called <strong>DRH-WUP</strong> exchanges data with the GamePad using a 5 GHz Wi-Fi signal.</li></ul></li><li>An <strong>Advanced Host Controller Interface</strong> (AHCI), revision 1.2, to connect to the <strong>Disc Drive</strong> using the SATA protocol.</li><li>A legacy <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/gamecube/#internal-io">External Interface (EXI)</a> to access the <strong>Real-Time Clock</strong> (RTC). According to fail0overflow, the EXI block is also attached to some MEM1 for backwards compatibility reasons <sup id="bibref:21"><a href="#bib:cpu-fail0verflow" role="doc-biblioref">[21]</a></sup>, allowing to emulate part of the legacy <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/gamecube/#operating-system">IPL ROM</a> using portions of MEM1.</li></ul><h4 id="the-supplemental-interface">The supplemental interface</h4><p>For another status-quo-breaking moment, let’s now go over some unusual features that the Wii U included, which at first no one knew what they would be used for.</p><div class="body-side"><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/mario_amiibo.d30d27df399fa6ccde2f239c929467fedfc35da3b0eb5d8e83471c62bd4ab1d8.png"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/mario_amiibo.d30d27df399fa6ccde2f239c929467fedfc35da3b0eb5d8e83471c62bd4ab1d8_hu_5672596bb027be09.webp 455w"><img class="title-image no-borders" alt="Image" width="455" height="481" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/mario_amiibo.d30d27df399fa6ccde2f239c929467fedfc35da3b0eb5d8e83471c62bd4ab1d8.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">An amiibo figurine of Mario related to the new Super Smash Bros title <sup id="bibref:22"><a href="#bib:games-marioamiibo" role="doc-biblioref">[22]</a></sup>.</figcaption></figure><p>When the Wii U reached the hand of users, they quickly noticed the GamePad had a <strong>Near-Field Communication</strong> (NFC) reader. Initially, Nintendo didn’t share the goals of such capabilities and some outlets even speculated that it would eventually enable NFC payments <sup id="bibref:23"><a href="#bib:io-nfc_note" role="doc-biblioref">[23]</a></sup>. It wasn’t until 2014 that Nintendo finally unveiled their intentions with NFC technology: Figurines, which they called <strong>amiibos</strong>. These embed a unique NFC tag <sup id="bibref:24"><a href="#bib:io-nfc_e3" role="doc-biblioref">[24]</a></sup> and games that support them allow the user to ‘scan’ their amiibo (by placing them on top of the reader area of the GamePad). Then, the game will detect which type of figurine is placed and react accordingly (i.e. unlock premium content, create a special avatar and so forth). Tags may also bundle small storage (just 512 Bytes <sup id="bibref:25"><a href="#bib:io-gamepad_brew" role="doc-biblioref">[25]</a></sup>) that games may use to store user data.</p></div><p>Overall, not only these figurines opened up another market for Nintendo but they also quickly turned into a rare collectible (for the enjoyment of scalpers). Though the market of these figurines wasn’t exactly ‘new’ as other companies like Activision and Disney were already commercialising this type of product.</p><hr><h2 id="operating-system">Operating System</h2><p>What if I tell you there are a total of <strong>four operating systems</strong> stored in this console? Two of them run in ‘Wii U’ mode, while the other two are only used for backwards compatibility.</p><p>As this topic can get very confusing, let’s start with the native Wii U-only systems.</p><h3 id="with-age-comes-wisdom">With age comes wisdom</h3><p>Just like in the original Wii, <strong>the Wii U runs two OSes</strong> concurrently, one in the CPU (Espresso) and another one in the I/O processor (Starbuck). However, both have been designed with thicker layers of abstraction and a more sophisticated security model. Hence, <strong>Wii U games do not run on bare metal</strong> anymore.</p><h4 id="starbucks-improved-os">Starbuck’s improved OS</h4><p>To start with, Starbuck’s operating system is now called <strong>IOSU</strong> (another name given by fail0verflow, meaning <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/wii/#starlets-os">IOS</a> + Wii U) and you will only find one variant of it. This means there’re no more <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/wii/#starlets-os">update slots</a>, although there’s an alternative IOSU referred to as ‘IOSU255’ which is only loaded when installing system updates.</p><p>IOSU is still composed of a <strong>multi-threaded microkernel</strong>, which is now able to allocate up to 180 threads (previously 100), along with <strong>drivers</strong> and <strong>modules</strong> to take care of I/O access and security.</p><p>One interesting aspect is that Starbuck disposes of two secured memory blocks for loading its kernel: Its internal <strong>96 KB of SRAM</strong> and <strong>3 MB of 1T-SRAM</strong> (known as ‘MEM0’) from the Wii GPU block. This is for performance and security reasons, as it prevents Starbuck from being exposed to tampering and reduces congestion.</p><h4 id="espressos-new-os">Espresso’s new OS</h4><p>First things first, Espresso now runs an actual operating system. That’s the most obvious change considering Wii games run on bare metal. This is called <strong>Cafe OS</strong> and it’s made of multiple components, not necessarily stored in the same medium <sup id="bibref:26"><a href="#bib:operating_system-cafe" role="doc-biblioref">[26]</a></sup>:</p><ul><li>A <strong>bootloader</strong> that bootstraps the system.</li><li>A <strong>Kernel</strong> that provides a layer of abstraction between the hardware (in this case, through Starbuck) and applications. In doing so, it runs under the highest privileges of the CPU and provides many low-level functions (memory management, security, etc). Curiously enough, this component runs on the middle core (Core 1) as it provides more cache <sup id="bibref:27"><a href="#bib:cpu-fail0verflow_espresso" role="doc-biblioref">[27]</a></sup>.</li><li><strong>User applications</strong> that run on top of the Kernel and provide functionality for the user. This includes the interactive shell, the game and other applications installed.</li></ul><p>Moving on, the Kernel runs in <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/playstation-3/#os-security-hierarchy">supervisor mode</a> and communicates with Starbuck using the same <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/wii/#starlets-os">Inter-Process Communication</a> (IPC) channel that the Wii relied on. This component can load multiple programs (processes) in memory, but it’s very limited in the number of processes it can run simultaneously (especially if they require foreground capabilities), I’ll talk more about it in a bit.</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/os_levels.3563981f5f6b36f3d78ccafcd7cace33e92dac03f6a11083c72d35197f02409b.png"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="762" height="519" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/os_levels.3563981f5f6b36f3d78ccafcd7cace33e92dac03f6a11083c72d35197f02409b.png" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Overview of the privilege levels in the Wii U, after combining both operating systems.</figcaption></figure><p>Cafe OS loads system and user applications using a proprietary binary structure called ‘RPL’, which is used for both executables and libraries. Moreover, the main executable is referred to as ‘RPX’. One of Cafe OS’ utilities, <code>Loader</code>, takes care of loading them up into memory (with the cooperation of IOSU) and executing them. <code>Loader</code> also performs <strong>dynamic linking</strong> to connect references of Cafe OS in the program with the physical Cafe OS installed in the console. Finally, applications are installed in the form of ‘channels’ which later show up in the ‘System Menu’ (the interactive shell).</p><p>Due to the way the Kernel organises the memory layout, the user is only able to run <strong>up to two types of programs</strong> at the same time. One is the ‘foreground’ program with the most amount of memory available (i.e. the game) and the other is a ‘background’ app with significantly less memory allocated (i.e. the web browser). The user may switch between the two without having to close either, but only one can be displayed at a time and, again, there can only be one ‘foreground’ and one ‘background’ app loaded. Otherwise, either gets closed/deallocated.</p><h4 id="the-big-cost">The big cost</h4><p>It’s time to address something that may sound a bit outrageous: <strong>Cafe OS consumes 1 GB to run</strong>, that’s half of MEM2 that was supposed to be available for games. This means that the Wii U, having featured the immense amount of 2 GB of DDR3, only grants 1 GB to the most important application that users care about.</p><p>In my <em>humble</em> opinion, this is a real disappointment, especially considering an operating system like Mac OS X 10.4 “Tiger”, which also runs on similar PowerPC CPUs, provided a more sophisticated set of features and only asked for a minimum of 256 MB of RAM. Even so, game console manufacturers tend to design their operating systems so they consume the least amount of footprint possible, and it seems Nintendo couldn’t fulfill that requirement this time. On a curious note, it was even reported that Nintendo planned to ship new versions of SDKs and software updates that would reduce memory consumption from the OS side. Yet, here we are, with its successor already in stores and no further production of Wii Us in sight. Oh well!</p><p>Be as it may, there’s a slight compromise: <strong>‘foreground’ apps may claim an extra 40 MB</strong> as long as they are being displayed (a.k.a shown in the foreground). However, as soon as the user switches to a background app, this block gets automatically deallocated. This is not exactly a ‘simple’ feature, leaving it up to developers to find good use.</p><h3 id="maintaining-traditions">Maintaining traditions</h3><p>It all changes when a Wii game is played, as the Wii U enters a state called <strong>‘Virtual Wii’ (vWii)</strong>. There’s no emulator present, but re-shuffled hardware that makes Wii games think they are running on the original platform.</p><p>To enter vWii mode, Starbuck executes a program called <code>cafe2wii</code> that takes care of morphing the console into a Wii (a.k.a de-activating all the modern features) <sup id="bibref:28"><a href="#bib:operating_system-cafe2wii" role="doc-biblioref">[28]</a></sup>. Now, there are different sets of binaries available to use (each with a variant of cafe2wii), specifically, <code>OSv0</code> and <code>OSv1</code>. The choice depends on the type of vWii mode needed. In summary:</p><ul><li><strong>Normal vWii</strong> launches the good-old <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/wii/#broadways-os">System Menu</a>, exactly what a real Wii does after pressing the power button. This is useful for playing a disc-based Wii game or for launching any <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/wii/#broadways-os">channel</a> installed.</li><li><strong>HAI vWii</strong> directly launches a Wii game (bypassing the System Menu). This is used for executing Wii games bought from the Virtual Console store. Hence, the Wii game may be installed in the Wii U’s dedicated storage (eMMC or external USB).</li></ul><p>Luckily, not all the modern hardware in vWii mode is wasted, as the GamePad can turn into a mirrored screen with a controller as well. If that’s not enough, the front of the GamePad contains infrared lights that behave as a <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/wii/#next-gen-controllers">sensor bar</a>, so Wii Remotes don’t require a TV at all.</p><p>Just like with any Nintendo console with backwards compatibility, once in Wii mode, the only way back is by rebooting the console.</p><h3 id="storage-medium">Storage Medium</h3><p>The Wii wasn’t shy in providing multimedia-centred storage options (the SD card was a nice addition). And so, the Wii U builds on top of that.</p><p>Having said that, let’s now see what storage options are spread throughout this console:</p><div class="tabs"><ul class="tab-links"><li id="tab-3-1-boot-roms-link" class="active"><a href="#tab-3-1-boot-roms">Boot ROMs</a></li><li id="tab-3-2-sensitive-roms-link"><a href="#tab-3-2-sensitive-roms">Sensitive ROMs</a></li><li id="tab-3-3-diversified-nand-link"><a href="#tab-3-3-diversified-nand">Diversified NAND</a></li><li id="tab-3-4-extra-storage-link"><a href="#tab-3-4-extra-storage">Extra storage</a></li></ul><div class="tab-content"><div class="tab active body-side" id="tab-3-1-boot-roms"><h4 id="tab-3-1-boot-roms" class="tab-title">Boot ROMs</h4><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/motherboard/soc_focus.4be5037c3307490262547382498c858f99ea61086b33613f4d6ff3eadeb9b917.jpg"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/motherboard/soc_focus.4be5037c3307490262547382498c858f99ea61086b33613f4d6ff3eadeb9b917_hu_f0831ea9cdf90c5c.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/motherboard/soc_focus.4be5037c3307490262547382498c858f99ea61086b33613f4d6ff3eadeb9b917_hu_f9842e2046338724.webp 800w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/motherboard/soc_focus.4be5037c3307490262547382498c858f99ea61086b33613f4d6ff3eadeb9b917_hu_5d09ebe6fc8ae3dc.webp 900w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="900" height="818" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/motherboard/soc_focus.4be5037c3307490262547382498c858f99ea61086b33613f4d6ff3eadeb9b917.jpg" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Within this complex package, there are two hidden ROMs storing boot code in plain form.</figcaption></figure><p>The 6th generation cemented the concept of an operating system in a video game console. Yet, the appliance was still exposed to the vulnerabilities resulting from combining off-the-shelf components with in-house ones. As console manufacturers couldn’t tailor the design of third-party chips, custom security components had to reside in separate locations within the motherboard, thereby being exposed to tampering and reverse engineering.</p><p>With the 7th generation, IBM presented a new range of PowerPC CPUs that embedded a hidden mask ROM within the silicon. This enabled the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 to house sensitive code in plain form (as CPUs only understand unencrypted code) without fear of being read by hackers. That being said, it’s now the turn for the Wii U so IBM also had something prepared for it: Inside Espresso, there is a hidden <strong>16 KB of ROM</strong> connected to one of the cores. This is used as the first boot stage of Espresso and, once it’s been executed, it makes sure subsequent binaries are approved by Nintendo.</p><p>Combined this with Starbuck’s own <strong>4 KB of Boot ROM</strong> (inherited from the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/wii/#boot-sequence">previous Wii model</a>), you’ve got two CPUs enforcing Nintendo’s security model as soon as they start up.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev pre">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-3-2-sensitive-roms">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-3-2-sensitive-roms"><h4 id="tab-3-2-sensitive-roms" class="tab-title">Sensitive ROMs</h4><p>Nintendo also bundled other ROMs scattered around Latte containing <em>very sensitive</em> information.</p><p>The first one is <strong>1 KB of One-Time-Programmable (OTP)</strong> memory where many encryption keys are stored. This memory was also found on the Wii but in a smaller size (128 Bytes). OTP stores the information used to encrypt/decrypt data and verify the integrity of existing data <sup id="bibref:29"><a href="#bib:operating_system-otp" role="doc-biblioref">[29]</a></sup>. It also stores flags for enabling/disabling low-level functionality of the motherboard (i.e. JTAG). Additionally, OTP is segregated between Espresso’s bank and Starbuck’s one <sup id="bibref:30"><a href="#bib:anti_piracy-keys" role="doc-biblioref">[30]</a></sup>, as both will need to read different keys and subsequently lock OTP access at different points in time.</p><p>The second is <strong>512 Bytes of SPI EEPROM</strong> (SEEPROM) which is writable (albeit not all of it is edited) and houses many configuration flags and miscellaneous meta-data <sup id="bibref:31"><a href="#bib:operating_system-seeprom" role="doc-biblioref">[31]</a></sup>. Some data in SEEPROM is encrypted with keys found in OTP memory.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-3-1-boot-roms">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-3-3-diversified-nand">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-3-3-diversified-nand"><h4 id="tab-3-3-diversified-nand" class="tab-title">Diversified NAND</h4><div class="tabs nested float-side"><ul class="tab-links nested"><li id="nestedtab-2-1-nand-link" class="active"><a href="#nestedtab-2-1-nand">NAND</a></li><li id="nestedtab-2-2-emmc-link"><a href="#nestedtab-2-2-emmc">eMMC</a></li></ul><figure class="tab active nested" id="nestedtab-2-1-nand"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/motherboard/nand.5dd0ce128e435664dc0df000a8f6185685749c1098af8c308a9a222262e585c4.jpg"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/motherboard/nand.5dd0ce128e435664dc0df000a8f6185685749c1098af8c308a9a222262e585c4_hu_7f2e2b2c739f5f56.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/motherboard/nand.5dd0ce128e435664dc0df000a8f6185685749c1098af8c308a9a222262e585c4_hu_a76d3d740ab1701a.webp 800w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/motherboard/nand.5dd0ce128e435664dc0df000a8f6185685749c1098af8c308a9a222262e585c4_hu_d025fabe9187ea66.webp 900w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="900" height="687" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/motherboard/nand.5dd0ce128e435664dc0df000a8f6185685749c1098af8c308a9a222262e585c4.jpg" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">NAND chip providing 1 GB of storage.</figcaption></figure><figure class="tab nested" id="nestedtab-2-2-emmc"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/motherboard/emmc.e417bb1af8169c8ee147cf25e17cbd4f298ce592d5a44ff456a21879790437a6.jpg"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/motherboard/emmc.e417bb1af8169c8ee147cf25e17cbd4f298ce592d5a44ff456a21879790437a6_hu_fa876e41db9cc922.webp 500w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/motherboard/emmc.e417bb1af8169c8ee147cf25e17cbd4f298ce592d5a44ff456a21879790437a6_hu_e87ebc07b1b415a3.webp 800w,
https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/motherboard/emmc.e417bb1af8169c8ee147cf25e17cbd4f298ce592d5a44ff456a21879790437a6_hu_15b0ccf3a081462d.webp 900w"><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="900" height="687" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/motherboard/emmc.e417bb1af8169c8ee147cf25e17cbd4f298ce592d5a44ff456a21879790437a6.jpg" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">eMMC chip providing 8 GB of storage (in this example).</figcaption></figure></div><p>Having talked about the low-level part of the system, let’s take a look now at where the ‘visible’ part is stored. There are two storage spaces found on the motherboard:</p><p>Firstly, we’ve got <strong>1 GB of NAND</strong> divided into two banks:</p><ul><li>The first 512 MB store the Wii U’s operating system (later-stage bootloaders and Cafe OS).</li><li>The second 512 MB house the software that makes up the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/wii/#operating-system">Wii’s operating system</a> (System menu, IOS slots and channels) except the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/wii/#boot-sequence">original bootloaders</a>.</li></ul><p>Secondly, either <strong>8 GB or 32 GB of embedded MultiMediaCard</strong> (eMMC) depending on the model purchased, is available for user data only (downloaded titles, DLCs and game updates). Remember this may also include Wii titles downloaded from the Virtual Console store (which can only be launched from the Wii U’s System Menu).</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-3-2-sensitive-roms">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next" href="#tab-3-4-extra-storage">Next »</a></div></div><div class="tab body-side" id="tab-3-4-extra-storage"><h4 id="tab-3-4-extra-storage" class="tab-title">Extra storage</h4><figure class="float-side"><a href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/hdd_usb.9e6a2cab35d2399868053099a38093b87c6dbab427bd0cf59c0e44ec6dd3e9af.jpg"><picture><img class="title-image" alt="Image" width="868" height="690" src="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/hdd_usb.9e6a2cab35d2399868053099a38093b87c6dbab427bd0cf59c0e44ec6dd3e9af.jpg" loading="lazy"></picture></a><figcaption class="caption">Typical external HDD connected to a USB Y cable so it works on the Wii U.</figcaption></figure><p>For those users that run out of space pretty quickly, the Wii U came with support for <strong>external USB storage</strong> out-of-the-box. The only limitations, however, are that the medium will have to be formatted using the Wii U’s proprietary file system and only user data can be stored. As a side note, the Wii U’s USB ports only output up to 500mA of current <sup id="bibref:32"><a href="#bib:operating_system-current" role="doc-biblioref">[32]</a></sup>, which ironically is not enough for typical USB HDDs (around 900mA). So, users had to resort to USB Y cables to combine the current of two USB ports.</p><p>Moving on, there’s also an <strong>SD card slot</strong>, but that’s only taken advantage of by certain programs and games that store exchangeable multimedia (such as images). Luckily, it supports FAT32 so no formatting will be needed.</p><div class="tab-navigation"><a rel="nofollow" class="prev" href="#tab-3-3-diversified-nand">« Previous</a>
<a rel="nofollow" class="next pre">Next »</a></div></div></div></div><h3 id="boot-process">Boot process</h3><p>Having two independent CPUs can be difficult the setup. Still, <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/nintendo-ds/#cpu">Nintendo is no stranger to this practice</a>. So, how does the Wii U manage to coordinate Espresso and Starbuck so the console ends up running an interactive shell on top of a secured environment? Let’s take a look.</p><h4 id="multicore-chaos">Multicore chaos</h4><p>Before we start I want to address the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/xbox-360/#multicore-chaos">same problem</a> that was present on other symmetric architectures like the Xbox 360: Symmetric cores must be coordinated so each one doesn’t take over the system at the same time. Well, Espresso adopts similar practices to x86, where only one core is activated upon switching on the CPU. Then, it’s up to the program loading in the master core to wake up the other two <sup id="bibref:33"><a href="#bib:cpu-fail0verflow_espresso" role="doc-biblioref">[33]</a></sup>.</p><p>Nonetheless, all cores contain the same reset vector. Consequently, the program is responsible for asking itself which type it is running from and then proceed based on the answer. This modus operandi is similar to ARMv7.</p><h4 id="boot-procedure">Boot procedure</h4><p>It’s time to see the boot routines and, let me tell you, they are not particularly simple. After all, it’s two independent processors with their unique security model being initialised in a serialised way, so that requires a lot of coordination. For simplicity’s sake, my summary is somewhat shortened to avoid feeding you up with lots of information, so don’t forget to check out the citations if you are curious for more.</p><p>On the other side, you don’t need to completely understand this to follow the rest of the article, so feel free to move on if it’s not your area of interest!</p><p>Alrighty, let’s begin already. Once the user presses the power button, the following happens <sup id="bibref:34"><a href="#bib:operating_system-boot" role="doc-biblioref">[34]</a></sup>:</p><ol style="list-style-type:decimal"><li>Starbuck wakes up and proceeds to…<ol style="list-style-type:decimal"><li>Execute code found in its reset vector (<code>0xFFFF0000</code>) <sup id="bibref:35"><a href="#bib:operating_system-boot0" role="doc-biblioref">[35]</a></sup>, which points to its mask ROM (where the first boot stage, <code>boot0</code>, is). The first routine tells Starbuck to copy <code>boot0</code> into Starbuck’s SRAM, so it runs faster.</li><li><code>boot0</code> then initialises part of the I/O and nearby blocks by reading the flags found on OTP memory and SEEPROM. It then proceeds to fetch the next bootloader stage (<code>boot1</code>) from NAND.</li><li><code>boot1</code> is encrypted and signed, so Starbuck first checks its signature (RSA type), the integrity of the content (by comparing the SHA-1 hashes) and then proceeds to decrypt it (using AES). All of the keys and certificates needed are fetched from OTP memory.</li><li>More I/O is initialised. Then, SEEPROM and part of OTP is locked down from being accessed again. Finally, <code>boot1</code> kicks off.</li><li><code>boot1</code> initialises even more I/O and prepares MEM2 and MEM0 for use <sup id="bibref:36"><a href="#bib:operating_system-boot1" role="doc-biblioref">[36]</a></sup>. It then transfers <code>IOSU Firmware</code> from NAND to MEM1 and performs the same verification & decryption process. If everything went well, Starbuck disables the used OTP memory and zeroes out sensitive data. Finally, it jumps to <code>IOSU Firmware</code>.</li><li><code>IOSU Firmware</code> is a collection of binaries. The first one launched is <code>IOSU Loader</code>, which moves the rest of the firmware (a.k.a <code>IOSU</code>) to specific memory locations (SRAM and MEM0). It then clears itself from MEM1 and jumps to SRAM, where <code>IOSU Kernel</code> awaits.</li><li>The <code>IOSU Kernel</code> first does a quick MEM1 check <sup id="bibref:37"><a href="#bib:operating_system-iosu" role="doc-biblioref">[37]</a></sup>, but after that finishes, that’s <strong>Starbuck up and running with IOSU</strong>. To perform its functions, IOSU’s modules are found on MEM0.</li><li>Espresso is next, so IOSU copies <code>Cafe OS</code> (in encrypted form) into MEM2 and kickstarts Espresso.</li></ol></li><li>The first core of Espresso powers on, then…<ol style="list-style-type:decimal"><li>The reset vector is at address <code>0x00000100</code>, which at this point is masked by the Boot ROM, so it starts execution there.</li><li>MMU, L1/L2 caches and registers are cleared. Then, Espresso switches to ‘Translated mode’ (activates <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/gamecube/#making-the-most-of-aram">virtual memory</a>).</li><li>By fiddling with locked L1 cache and empty memory writes, the BootROM is copied to L1 (to run faster) without reaching external RAM.</li><li>The reset vector becomes an infinite loop (to prevent intruders from attempting to <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/xbox-360/#tab-13-1-the-glitcher">reset the CPU</a>).</li><li>AES keys from OTP are copied into L1. Then, OTP is disabled.</li><li><code>Cafe OS Kernel</code>’s header is copied to L1 and its signature is verified using the stored keys.</li><li><code>Cafe OS Kernel</code>’s data is hashed and decrypted by using the DMA engine to send blocks to L1 back and forth.</li><li>The now-unencrypted <code>Cafe OS Kernel</code>, in RAM, is mapped and ready for execution. L1 and L2 are flushed; and the Boot ROM is disabled. Finally, execution jumps to <code>Cafe OS Kernel</code>.</li><li>Espresso, now running <code>Cafe OS Kernel</code>, checks configuration files that instruct it to launch the <code>System Menu</code> application.</li><li><code>System Menu</code> is fetched from NAND into MEM2 and processed like any other encrypted binary. If that goes well, <code>System Menu</code> is launched.</li></ol></li><li>The <strong>user is now in control</strong>!</li></ol><h4 id="vwii-boot-process">vWii boot process</h4><p>As soon as a Wii title is launched, the system proceeds with an ‘extra’ loader stage that turns the Wii U into a Wii. The process starts with Starbuck executing <code>cafe2wii</code>, which proceeds to <sup id="bibref:38"><a href="#bib:cpu-fail0verflow" role="doc-biblioref">[38]</a></sup>:</p><ol style="list-style-type:decimal"><li>Reboot Espresso.</li><li>Slow down Espresso and disable the two extra cores.</li><li>Upload a firmware for the DMCU video encoder.</li><li>Upload the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/wii/#maintaining-compatibility">old fonts</a> into an area of MEM1, which can them be accessed from the EXI interface (to replicate <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/gamecube/#internal-io">the old EXI route</a>).</li><li>Activate a compatibility mode on the AHCI interface (where the SATA disc drive is connected to) so it can be commanded using the old <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/gamecube/#internal-io">Disc Interface</a> (DI) protocol.</li><li>Copy the keys from OTP memory to its internal SRAM, as vWii will think the internal SRAM is the <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/wii/#broadways-os">legacy SEEPROM</a>.</li><li>Disable Wii U-exclusive I/O, except the GamePad (unless it’s deactivated by the user or game metadata).</li><li>Boot IOS. The choice of <a href="https://www.copetti.org/writings/consoles/wii/#starlets-os">IOS slot</a> depends on the vWii mode used and, if in HAI mode, the game.<ul><li>The IOS package for vWii has been slightly modified with additional modules. This includes <code>DI2SD</code> to emulate the disc drive and <code>OHCI1</code> to translate the input from the GamePad into Bluetooth commands (thus, replicating the Wii Remote controller) <sup id="bibref:39"><a href="#bib:operating_system-hai" role="doc-biblioref">[39]</a></sup>.</li></ul></li><li>Upload either the <code>Wii System Menu</code> or <code>NAND Boot Program</code> (the binary that runs Wii titles) to MEM2, the choice depends on the vWii mode used.<ul><li>As Espresso will have booted from its boot ROM first, it will only accept binaries using the Wii U’s security model. Therefore, both Wii binaries have been modified to comply with this.</li></ul></li><li>Kickstart Espresso and let it process and run the designated binary.</li><li>The user is now in control (again!).</li></ol><h3 id="interactive-shell">Interactive shell</h3><p>The Wii U’s graphical user interface is called <strong>System Menu</strong> (or ‘Wii U Menu’) which, as you’ve seen before, it’s an application launched right after Cafe OS finishes loading.</p><p>Most of the services that the Wii U offers (i.e. disc game launcher, settings, online store, etc) are found in the form of foreground applications, the user can pick either from the System Menu. On the other side, a small set of functions (like an <strong>Internet Browser</strong>) are implemented as background applications and can only be launched from the ‘Home’ menu.</p><div class="side-by-side"><figure class="toleft"><a class="toleft" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/screenshots/home_drc.6990b4aaa20368896b617295c33030671bfc36773d470bb7976eea9f94eb7f99.jpg"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/screenshots/home_drc.6990b4aaa20368896b617295c33030671bfc36773d470bb7976eea9f94eb7f99_hu_cdf7f34a2aac4249.webp 500w,

The last function, however, is only available for Wii games purchased from the eShop (part of the Virtual Console catalogue).</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/gamepad_vwii.7187f26c83900aeb558b2468647bccac2cadbb4d262194c220f15b052ee1f89a.jpg"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/photos/gamepad_vwii.7187f26c83900aeb558b2468647bccac2cadbb4d262194c220f15b052ee1f89a_hu_f759b91c56beb8e5.webp 500w,

In doing so, new accessories can be supported, apart from improving the software and/or patching system vulnerabilities.</p><figure class="centered-container"><a class="centered-container" href="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/screenshots/updates.98318760fecf2478a5f345a4ad0fd0873c94f184ff5a04e7be60f4c59048c31c.jpeg"><picture><source type="image/webp" srcset="https://www.copetti.org/images/consoles/wiiu/screenshots/updates.98318760fecf2478a5f345a4ad0fd0873c94f184ff5a04e7be60f4c59048c31c_hu_fa9ed4e29694e29f.webp 500w,
